subject: history_social
passage: During the siege of Paris in 1870 and 1871, the city was cut off from the rest of France. Homing pigeons carried messages into the city, and to fit more words onto each bird, the messages were photographed and shrunk onto tiny sheets of film. Historian Claude Mbeki hypothesizes that most of these messages were personal notes from families to relatives inside Paris rather than official government dispatches.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Mbeki's hypothesis?

choices.A: Most surviving pigeon messages are short private notes, such as news of births and word that relatives were well.
choices.B: Each tiny sheet of film could hold thousands of separate messages, far more than earlier pigeon mail.
choices.C: The great majority of the surviving messages are orders and reports exchanged between military officers in the field.
choices.D: Government offices in Paris kept detailed records of every pigeon that arrived in the city during the siege.

explanation.why: Mbeki's hypothesis is about the content of the messages: personal notes rather than official dispatches. The strongest support would come from looking at the messages themselves and finding that most are private family news. Facts about how the messages were carried or recorded do not settle what they said.
explanation.A: Correct. If most surviving messages are private family notes, the messages were mainly personal, as Mbeki claims.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The capacity of the film says nothing about whether the messages were personal or official.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Messages that are mostly military orders would show the opposite of what Mbeki claims.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Records of pigeon arrivals do not tell us what kinds of messages the pigeons carried.
